title: Computational irreducibility makes short theorems with only long proofs inevitable

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Computational irreducibility makes short theorems with only long proofs inevitable

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because the proof processes of almost every area of mathematics are computationally irreducible, adding axioms cannot remove the problem: there will essentially always be theorems that are short to state but whose shortest proofs are very long.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But I suspect that ultimately there is almost always computational irreducibility, and this makes it essentially inevitable that there will be short theorems that only allow long proofs.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), p. 779. Scope: axiom systems of mathematics, idealized as multiway systems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-30: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Proof complexity provides precise restricted versions and some checkable lower bounds, while formal corpora support empirical exploration. Neither current corpora nor known theory establish the sweeping inevitability claim across axiom systems.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix a formal theory, proof calculus, theorem-length measure, and proof-length bound, then exhibit short theorem families with proven lower bounds on their shortest proofs. Compare the result across theories and axiom extensions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Existing proof corpora contain found proofs, not certified shortest proofs.

The assertion covers almost every area of mathematics.

Proof length is calculus- and encoding-dependent.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: It is a standard theorem, represented in public proof libraries for arithmetic and related systems, that sufficiently strong theories have statements with no short proofs, and that finitely many extra axioms do not restore a computable bound. The sentence says this holds because almost every area of mathematics is computationally irreducible. That explanatory quantifier is outside the classical theorem and is not checked by one formalization.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In a fixed system that represents arithmetic, ask whether for every computable bound there is a theorem whose shortest proof exceeds that bound. A positive proof confirms the length claim for that system; a uniform short-proof procedure would refute it. Extending the result to almost every area needs a separate argument for each area.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Extra axioms can shorten particular proofs while leaving no uniform short bound.

The classical theorem covers systems that represent computation, and almost every area needs a further argument.

Existence of long proofs is weaker than computational irreducibility of the whole proof process.
